utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.x

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. We are starting late, we were scheduled to start at 10.00 in any case. But we are starting later for the simple reason that I've had a short meeting with the ICTY doctor and also another official to make sure that it's safe to sit in this courtroom today following the discovery of the legionella bacterium in the water cooling towers of this institution. I am told that all measures that were needed have been taken over the weekend; and that although a final test will be carried out on Wednesday, that's in two days' time, we are certainly -- this courtroom is safer today than it was or it might have been on Thursday and Friday. That's the position as I have it. But I wanted to bring this to your information and I'm leaving everyone free to withdraw from the courtroom if he or she so desires, feeling that it may be -- we feel that we can continue, but we are only speaking for ourselves. So that's the position. I know that there are some preliminaries or some matters that you would like to address us about. There is one that I better raise now, because otherwise I will forget it. Mr. McCloskey, you remember the brief exchange we had when we were -- came back to you actually on one of your motions, protective measures, for a number of witnesses. And we told you there is a discrepancy between when you were seeking and what they had been granted before, and you then filed a revised annex A with the last column specifying the protective measures now being requested, putting us also in a position where we could compare with the previous two cases, Blagojevic and Krstic, and you were glad that we check on you. We check even twice; and since we were advised at the end of last week who the next witnesses are going to be after Major Rutten finishes testimony, I've discovered the following: Witness number 70 - and it's easy to explain what happened - following your revised assessment, you said, "Same as in Blagojevic." In Blagojevic, this witness was granted pseudonym, but he was a 92 bis witness who had testified in Krstic. And in Krstic, he hadn't testified with a pseudonym only, as indicated in annex -- readvised annex A, but I found out that he had also testified with face distortion. So I think it's the case of Prosecution amending its request, because it means basically that our decision, pursuant to your request, amends the protective measures that govern this person. And we need to rectify, we need to rectify that. The same applies to Witness number 80. Again, you said, "Same as in Blagojevic." Blagojevic indeed he had pseudonym only, but again this was a Rule 92 bis witness. I found out that in Krstic, he not only had a pseudonym but he also had facial and voice distortion. So we need to rectify this as well. I mean, I don't want a response from you. I'm sure you will verify this, come back to us, possibly later on today, so that we hand down an oral decision amending our previous written decision. Because in relation to 70 and 80, we have just identified pseudonym and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. Nicholls identified the problem with 70, who is the next witness, as you know, and I think he has mentioned that to Defence counsel. So that is an immediacy that we appreciate you identifying and as the witness would like that, he's told us that he would like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So I was working on the assumption that the witness hasn't renounced to these previous protective measures. I mean, if I am wrong, obviously my assumption, you will let us know. Yes. Now I understand there are some -- some of you would like to address the Chamber. Mr. Bourgon, welcome back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges. Good morning to my colleagues on the other sides of the courtroom. Mr. President, we've had an opportunities to examine the Prosecution motion for protective measures, which was filed on 28 November. And preliminary consideration is that in order to avoid any delay in the proceedings, we will have no objections with witness number 70 testifying pursuant to protective measures. That being said, Mr. President, I'm now in a position to confirm that on behalf of all Defence teams, that the Prosecution motion filed on 28 November does raise some serious concerns which we believe need to be addressed without delay. Accordingly, Mr. President, we figure that this calls for a three-fold Defence response. And with your permission, first, I would begin by highlighting some general principles which we respectfully submit should guide the Trial Chamber when deciding whether or not to grant or to order protective measures. Secondly, my colleagues representing the accused Miletic and Beara will address the specifics of the Prosecution motion; and, thirdly, the Defence will file a written joint response for the consideration of the Trial Chamber. With your leave, Mr. President, I will begin with those general principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The practice that we have adopted here is that we try to avoid as much as possible taking from sitting time to deal with procedural matters that are not of the utmost urgency. So what I suggest is that if you have submissions to make that you draw them up in writing, and then we'll give them all due consideration with shortening of time limits if necessary, Mr. Bourgon. But, otherwise, we would have this witness waiting in the waiting room, when this is probably the last day that he has available to give evidence before being called back to his duties. You were not here last week, but we had to struggle to make him stay here or keep him here on Monday to finish his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I fully understand, and we will endeavour to put those general principles into our written response. However, we do believe that at this time that it is important for us to at least highlight some of the specific concerns that we have with the Prosecution motion, and I would invite you, Mr. President, to allow my colleague for Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, do not make us take more of the sitting time. We've already -- we started at 10.00. We haven't started this basically the sitting as yet, and we have a witness that needs to finish today. And this witness is here today, because we decided to allow each and every Defence team as much time as you required to properly cross-examine this witness. Yes, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I think the confusion may be that the Court invited the Defence to raise this issue Monday morning in last week' session, so we wanted to do that. And we can wait certainly and we'll wait until this witness passes, or at a time that's convenient. And that's why we thought it was appropriate to raise it immediately, but we understand the Court and we can I think hold off until whenever the court deems it appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, no, no, no, no, no. What the court had told you, Mr. Ostojic, was that since we are pressed for time, and particularly since one of the witnesses would start mid-week, Tuesday or Wednesday at the latest, we asked you to come possibly with a common response by today. Either by last Friday, when we were not sitting in writing or today, but that, with a view to know whether you were agreeing or objecting. If you are objecting, it's still until today. In other words, we want it in writing, and we will require to have it now. Since you are not objecting to Witness number 70, we can delay it until tomorrow. But the whole idea was to -- but let's not take more of the sitting time. I mean the idea was to know whether you objected or not, particularly since in the past you have not objected. Yes, Ms. Fauveau, I understand you also had some matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I will also present a written motion like my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for your cooperation. Who was the third? All right. Okay. All right. Yes. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Thayer, can we bring the witness in? Let's escort the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Major.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with your cross-examination and hopefully finish with you today. Mr. Lazarevic was cross-examining you when we needed to adjourn last Thursday. Mr. Lazarevic, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Major Rutten.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we broke off last Thursday, we were dealing with what happened at the meadow when you said you found nine bodies. I would now like to continue my examination with regard to these events. In your statement, you mentioned that on that meadow where you were, there was a certain number of documents. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a look at those documents, you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some -- I saw some which were picked up by the sergeant major, but I had not a close look on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell me how many documents there were, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see whether there were any photographs on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were IDs with photographs; that was what I saw. And I don't recollect if there were any with or without -- I did -- as I said before, I didn't examine them thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Koster perhaps examine them more thoroughly than you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That could have been, but I asked the Sergeant Major van Schaik to pick them up, and he had them in his hand. So he saw them much better than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you say that, to the best of your recollection, these were IDs, did you perhaps compare those documents to the bodies that you found on the meadow, as you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did -- as I said before, I didn't look at them fairly clearly. That was something the sergeant major did, so I can't -- I can't say that either I have compared those with the men who laid in the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then we can conclude that you do not know, in actual fact, whether these documents belonged to the people whose bodies you found on that meadow, the nine bodies you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't deny, nor can I conclude the same thing as you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. At one moment you heard a gunshot and you left that meadow, and van Schaik threw those documents somewhere along the way. Was that the way it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were more -- there was more gun fire, but the thing that you said about the sergeant major is correct, I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Right. As far as I managed to see from your statement - that is 3D37, on page 4, last paragraph - you said that you told van Schaik to throw away the documents, because you were afraid for your security. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: However, in the debriefing on the 6th of September 1995 - that is 3D42, on page 2 of the English version - you say that van Schaik threw the documents away on his own, of his own accord, because he was afraid. So what is correct? Did you order him to throw them away, or did he do it of his own accord because he was afraid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In such a situation, there happened things, simultaneously, so I said to him and probably he already -- he already thought of the same situation that could have happened as I did. So we were in the same unit, so you don't have to say much against each other to know what you have to do. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Further on you said that you returned to base by helping carry the stretchers, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me now where you found those stretchers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't found any stretchers. There were a lot of soldiers from DutchBat were helping people through the blockade, people who were injured, and were working there next to the road, medical personnel. And as in the moment, we saw that it was easy for us, as a DutchBater, to help them so we could easily get through the blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps the question was put wrongly or perhaps the interpretation was inappropriate. I didn't you say that you sort of found them somewhere. Where did you come across those persons who had the stretchers, the persons you joined in order to get to the base? How far away is the base, actually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the other side of the four APCs of the blockade. It's a few hundred metres, probably 200, I think. And it was next to the road that lead through the blockade of the four APCs that stood there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I think that -- well, roughly, that is a rather detailed explanation, 200 metres away from the APCs, but in the direction that is opposite to the base; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: These stretchers that you joined, did they have any wheels or rollers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were stretchers that were carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But these were stretchers belonging to the DutchBat, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was carrying these stretchers when you joined them? Was it Dutch soldiers who were carrying them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More of them were Dutch soldiers and some personnel of MSF.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. And who was on the stretchers? Were these empty stretchers, or were there some persons there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some persons on the stretcher. There was one person on the stretcher, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Was this a member of the DutchBat perhaps or somebody you did not know in uniform and civilian clothing? Can you tell us a bit more about that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was someone in civilian clothing, one of the Muslim population that were around the bus remise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And, practically, you were helping have that person brought to the Dutch base. Was the person carried into the Dutch base?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We brought the person near the car wash, because at the car wash there was a post of DutchBat with medical personnel stationed at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And that's where you left that person. What did you do then? Did you take the stretcher to the base, or did you leave the stretcher there, too? And did the three of you just go to the base on your own? How did all of this end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left the stretcher at that place near the car wash with the medical personnel. They cared for the person who was on the stretcher. And I went back towards the base, and there I met the Lieutenant Colonel Karremans, who was also near the APC blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Just one more question in relation to this: From where were they carrying this person? Can you tell me that? From where was that person being carried when you joined up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that specifically, because I don't know. It just -- the stretcher came by, and we hooked just on to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move on to another topic. You testified on the 5th of April this year [as interpreted] in the Krstic case, and your testimony from that case was admitted into evidence in this case, too. On page 21 from the Krstic case, you said that during the course of the day -- it's 2121. I apologise. And here also it says this year, it's on April 2000. That's a correction for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you testified there that during the course of the day, Serb soldiers were threatening you, that you had to hand over weapons, your radio communications equipment, and your armour; and then you said, "[In English] They were coming in; we were threatened. And I, at first, had to give up my weapon and my vest and the rest of my things." [Interpretation] On the next page of the transcript, you describe the circumstances under which your equipment was taken away from you. And as you describe that you said, "[In English] He moved his gun on my head at the rear side and said, 'I know your communication set now.'" . [Interpretation] Do you remember your testimony in the Krstic case in relation to these events? Did you have occasion to look at the transcript during your proofing or while you were getting ready to testify here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason why you handed over your weapons on that occasion and equipment was the fact that that soldier pointed a gun at you. Was that the reason why you decided to hand over your weapons and your equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldier was somewhat earlier also with me to -- that I had to deliver my equipment, but I said, "Look for your commander, because I'm not dealing with you." And later on, the commander came and the same soldier, and the -- he said, "Give up your things and your communication set and so on." I denied that, but -- and I turned my back against him, and then he pointed a gun at me. And at the moment I turned again, I saw the gun pointed at me and said, "okay," and then the soldier already took my things; and then just before that, I had a few seconds' time. And that was the reason I turned, because I could give a message to the battalion or at least to the other company that I was being held and I had to deliver my things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Basically my question is far more simple, and I think it requires a lot less explanation. The reason why a gun was pointed at you, was that a serious threat? And was that the reason why you handed over your equipment and your weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a serious threat, because the first time the soldier was with me I could send him away. But the second time before the gun was pointed, it was already loaded because he brought the bullet in the chamber of his weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. So I can understand that the reason why you decided at one point in time to do that was the fact that a gun was pointed at you and that you took that as a serious threat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to draw your attention to an earlier event. When you talk about events that had occurred somewhat before the event that we have just discussed, you testified about that in -- on page 2119, lines 6 through 9. And you talked about the first incident between you and a group of Serb soldiers; and on that page that I quoted, this is what you say: "[In English] I grabbed my weapon. I pointed at the Serbs; and at that time, they let go of my personnel so they could get back to me." [Interpretation] So at one moment that precedes this event, you pointed your weapon at a Serb soldier. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that a threat with weapons, pointing a weapon at someone, is of the same intensity, regardless of whether it is a Serb soldier or a member of a Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You point -- you give here a situation that is different. Because that event you spoke about was -- happened earlier that day, and was because they were not only looting our personal gear at some broken bus on the bus remise, but they also -- and I was sending two of my soldiers, because they were looting our personal things, and those two soldiers were held. And at that moment there was gunfire coming from the hill towards the bus, and there was a certain -- a rise of panic between the two Serb soldiers that were looting there. And the moment that I saw that, I went to them with my weapon pointed at the Serb soldiers from some distance, that they had to leave my men because they were using my two men as a form of a shield. And at that moment that that happened, that was the reason that I interfered. And I pointed the weapon towards the Serbs. Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm well aware of this. This is in your testimony in the Krstic case when you described the event. I'm just drawing your attention to the fact that at one point in time, you pointed your gun in the direction of a Serb soldier. And I asked you, was that a threat to their security just as much as it was a threat to your security when they pointed their gun at you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I described it before, it was a total different situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm just suggesting what the most obvious reason was for you to be disarmed. However, all members of the DutchBat were not disarmed at that time. You know for instance that Lieutenant Koster never surrendered his weapon. You remember that. He had his rifle on him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, but he was on the road next to a lot of cameras and I was on the side of the -- of the bus remise. So there were a lot of difficulties at our side, and I was not the only officer that got disarmed. My group what was -- was disarmed and also some other personnel of DutchBat were disarmed in that following hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you will agree with me that many others were not disarmed, who were also members of the DutchBat. I'm just trying to establish the reason for some being disarmed and others not. And I am suggesting that the reason was that you had threatened the Serb soldiers. Now, let us locate this in time. This was happening on the 12th of July, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So this incident, when you were disarmed, did this happen before General Mladic's arrival or after his arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After his arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In this connection, you see, there is a videotape which has been admitted into evidence, and this is Prosecution Exhibit P02047. And on this recording, I shall try to deal with some technical problems because it will take some time for my case manager to be able to arrange this. One can see a larger number of Dutch soldiers with weapon. Are you aware of that? Would you like us to take a look together at this recording?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, if you want to proceed with it, let's proceed with it. I mean you're asking him to know whether he would like or wouldn't like --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. If he remembers, that was my question, but if he doesn't, I mean, we have no problem with looking at this footage. It seems that we have some difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think we are ready now. I saw it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Lazarevic, if I could be of some help. If the purpose of this whole exercise is to get a confirmation from the witness whether it is correct that at this particular point in time that you are referring to there were several members of DutchBat carrying weapons, perhaps you can ask him the question. And he can tell you whether he grease or not, in which case you will not need the video any more, then. Yes, Mr. Thayer, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to slow things down. But if we are given a time, we can call up the movie on Sanction and show it that way. And we have got it queued up. I think we know from the exhibit list the clip that Mr. Lazarevic wants to show. I just leave it at that. I'm happy to save time, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Lazarevic can perhaps tell you -- tell us whether he would like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe the best situation would be to ask the witness whether he can confirm that a number of DutchBat members were armed at the time; and if not, then we can proceed. It seems that now it's okay. I believe we can show this to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That was what I wanted to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this was a recording broadcast by Reuters, and it happened after General Mladic 's arrival; and according to your testimony, this happened after you and your group were disarmed. Have you just seen a large number of members of the DutchBat carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe their --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, I don't believe this was this witness's testimony. I believe he testified he was disarmed after General's Mladic's arrival.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what he had testified, because you had a previous direct question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Then I apologise. I apologise. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you did see a large number of members of DutchBat who were armed even after General Mladic arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And not to dwell on this issue further, may we note that some were disarmed, but a large number were left with their weapons and equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe at this time we need a good date and time frame for this question to be intelligible on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, the -- you seem to be referring all the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you can be very specific about timing, because I would imagine that some -- not everyone that was disarmed was disarmed at the same time. So I think we need to be specific. You seem to be concentrating on the time after the arrival of Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can clarify with the witness, although it is already in his transcript in Krstic case, where he said that it was afternoon somewhere, at 12.00, when he saw General Mladic. And this is a period from, well, let's say something like 12.00, 1.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, are we talking about the same time period now, that is from the moment you saw General Mladic, about noon, when he was in the same location as you, and the next hour or two after that? Are we talking about that time frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. More or less, you're talking of the same time frame, yes. Can I see the text on my screen again? Thank you. It's already done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now move on to another issue. The events in Srebrenica took place quite sometime ago. Can we agree in general terms that your memory of the events in Srebrenica was fresher immediately after the events than in the year 2000 and today in the year 2006?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in general. You can say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, you could not describe the appearance of the commander of the unit that captured you, because you said they didn't wear any insignia. This can be found in the questionnaire that you filled in in 1995. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question -- that wasn't -- as I recall it, it wasn't asked whether I knew the commander or not. There was called whether I knew what unit it was and if I knew what units were acting in the enclave; and that was then the question to that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that again later, of course. But in the transcript, in the Krstic case, pages 21 to 23 of the transcript -- 2123-- you said it was Captain Mane who said that you could go back to your base after having spent sometime without your weapons and that two soldiers escorted you to the base. Mr. Rutten, the fact is that the name of Captain Mane is mentioned by you for the first time on the 5th of April 2000 in the Krstic case. I have carefully looked through your statements, your debriefings, but the name of Captain Mane never appeared until the Krstic case. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name of -- that could have been but the name of captain Mane was earlier named by other colleagues during the days in the enclave. And the reason why it's not in the different questionnaires or reports don't mean that Mane, Captain Mane was never named by me or other colleagues. It just wasn't a question to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Is that the answer to my question? My question was: Did you mention him? Leave -- let us leave aside for a moment the testimony of others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he just answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we take a look at 3D40, that is the number it can carries in the system. And this is the questionnaire which all members of the UN forces were asked to fill in. On pages 1 and 2 of that document, you say that you were captured by the Bosnian Serb army, and you said that these soldiers said that they belonged to special police forces of the army; and that you couldn't describe the appearance of the commanders, because these soldiers did not give their names, nor did they carry any insignia. You also said that you were not physically attacked or mistreated. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you abide by that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is that they asked something else in that questionnaire than I think than you're asking me now. Could you describe to me again your question now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Oh, yes. Perhaps it would be much better for the witness to take a look at the document itself. It's 3D40, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's next page, I think. But maybe it would be better just to -- just one question regarding this first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major Rutten, do you recognise your handwriting on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we take a look at the next page? Can we go down, down, a bit down and then next page, please. Okay, the last part of this page is what I was referring to. No. I apologise. That's not the one that I want. Can we go back to second page for one moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you see here on page 2 -- [In English]. ...and they stated that they belonged to a special police force of the army. [Interpretation] And then below AK 47 you find the following words, I can't describe any of it because they didn't tell their names [In English] or any insignia. [Interpretation] And then on the next page, in answer to a question, "Were you threatened with any harm, if you disobey, [In English] resisted your captors, what exactly was said?" "We were treated well." And then after that there was a question, "Were you physically attacked or maltreated by your captors at the time; if so describe what happened and then injuries sustained." You answered, "No." [Interpretation] Were these your answers given in that questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And do you stand by the answers you gave at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the debriefing to the Royal Dutch Army, Exhibit 3D42, on page 3, last paragraph of the English version, you state that you saw Serb civilians entering Srebrenica in various vehicles, carrying away goods in those vehicles. Do you remember saying that in the debriefing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And when you saw those people who came to examine those goods, did you notice whether they opened those rucksacks and carried away everything of value?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't study them while they were taking the things, but they were loading everything on to wheelbarrows, carriages, cars, whatever they found.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: During the examination last week, you said that there were many things in the base, along the road, around the "White House," and everywhere where there were refugees. I would just like to ask you two things in this connection. The first is: Those things that were left behind in the base, did the refugees decide to leave them on their own before they boarded the buses, or were they told by someone that they had to leave those things behind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends where that happened. If it was along the road where the refugees were assembled to go by groups, by 60 or 70 to go to the buses and they carried a lot of things, they were told by the Serbs to leave it there, or sometimes they took it out of their hands. And if you refer to the "White House," later on or further down the bus line, then they were told to leave everything outside the "White House" on the pile I described last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was thinking of the third case, neither of these two. I was thinking of the compound, the things that were left within the compound. Did any of the Dutch soldiers tell the refugees to leave their own things in the base?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which compound are you now speaking about? On the Bravo compound in Srebrenica or the compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Potocari.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people were never told to leave something on Dutch command. They were told to take their things, and they were given some extra things, even though. So I don't understand where you're referring to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the fact that many things were left within the base that belonged to the refugees. Is your answer that they left those things on their own accord?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had to leave them because they couldn't carry them any more. So it must have been on their own accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. That is my opinion, too. This pile of things was the object of a search by people who had come in various vehicles, who searched those things, and took away anything of any value; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But now you're connecting the things that are in the Potocari base, you're connecting that with the pile I described outside of the "White House," and that -- these are two different occasions. And I described in my earlier statement the situation near the pile and near the buses and though -- and also with the pile with the "White House." So there have never been Serbian people taking things from out of the Potocari compound itself; the moment we were there, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. That's what I'm saying, that they didn't enter the Potocari base, but that they looted things along the road next to the "White House" and close to the bus remise. Is that your testimony? So your saying that it was outside the base that people were looting things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you exclude the possibility that the people who were looting were also the people who set fire to what remained after they had collected everything of value?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is -- I can't exclude that possibility, neither can I confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your statement to the Dutch military police on the 2nd of August 1995, that was shortly after the events - this is Exhibit 3D41 - in paragraph 3, you said that you saw Serbs searching through the goods of deported men about 11.00 on the 14th of July. And you said that a pile of clothes, passports and other things, were set on fire. You said that the fire was burning for roughly one day. So that is more or less in accordance with what you said here. I just wish you to confirm that this was happening on the 14th, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must have been happened during the 14th, but the connection that you make between -- in that sentence between the men, the Serbian people who were looting the things and who -- who actually already set fire to the pile, that is something that I cannot confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't expect you to do that. I just would like you to confirm something that another member of the DutchBat testified to in connection with this event, if possible. And he said that when those things were burned, a considerable amount of ammunition exploded, which was among that pile, and you made photographs of that pile burning. Did you hear explosions of ammunition that was among those goods belonging to the refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw ammunition when I watched the pile a day earlier. And I never hear -- heard ammunition explode during the burning of the pile in front of the "White House." And I'm certain that I never heard that, because that would arose my attention then. So, no, I don't think so that that happened; but, okay, that's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Is that to say that what the other member of the DutchBat testified to is not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that here, because it could have been a different situation and a different pile and totally somewhere else. So you're asking me to draw a conclusion with no facts or details. I cannot do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to a different topic now. Again, we are on the 13th. We are going back to the 13th from the 14th, and we are going back to the episode between you and Mr. Van Duijn, who was then a Lieutenant. At one point in time, on the 13th of July, there was a misunderstanding between the two of you. And on that occasion, you held something against him; namely, his participation in the evacuation of refugees. Do you remember what I'm talking about? Do you remember that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When speaking about these events before the parliamentary commission - that is 3D39, on page 14, and it's the last paragraph - and as you were speaking directly about the separation of the men and van Duijn's role, you said the following, I'm going to quote now. "[In English] Groups were assembled at one location, and a few hundred metres away the people were directed to the buses. I had already observed that morning that the men and women were being separated in the area in between. Van Duijn did not have a direct view of this." [Interpretation] Is this the way you remember that, that van Duijn did not have a view of this, could not see what was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, because he was just next -- standing next to the four APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, you got into an argument with Serb soldiers and you used the term "Nazi methods." You said Nazi practice, actually, which led to a very harsh reaction on the part of the Serb soldiers who refused to continue participating in that. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question that you ask, "refused continuing participating in that?" I don't understand that. Could you address that question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I apologise. I will clarify it. [Interpretation] They refused to continue their participation in the evacuation of civilians from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And you mean with "they," the Serb soldiers to continue their participation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. But -- yeah, I must laugh because it isn't a laughable situation, because how come they didn't want to participate because they were in control? We were unable to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. Let's bring up 3D39, please. Initially, your first question was whether he could remember what you were alleging in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] That was my first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think I need to stop what's happening straight away by referring the witness to what is allegedly contained in this document. So let's bring it up. Is it up?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have stenographers minutes of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can explain. I did quote one part of the document. But then after that, what I'm discussing now with the witness about participation of Serb soldiers about his incident with soldiers calling these methods as Nazi practice is not contained in this document. It comes from another testimony before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Another person's testimony or his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It has to do with the testimony of another DutchBat member who appeared before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, there is a discussion in this, on the very next page, concerning this Nazi practices issue. I just wanted to clarify that for the record. He is asked to elaborate on that on page 15 of this parliamentary inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is perturbing me somewhat is when I read back your first question, which, to my understanding, arose out of 3D39. I'm referring you to page 25, line 19. And your question was at one point in time,"You got into an argument with Serb soldiers and you used the term Nazi methods. You said Nazi practice, which led to a very hard reaction on the part of the Serb soldiers who refused to continue participating in that. Do you remember that?" And then the witness told you that he couldn't understand what you were asking. And then immediately say,"They refused to continue their participation in the evacuation of civilians from Potocari." And you are obviously referring to the Serbian soldiers, but you're also referring, as I understand it, to something which the witness allegedly stated in this previous statement. So I think we need to eliminate any source of confusion here. And if you are referring to anything specific, please let's show it to the witness and move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay. This particular part is not what was contained. It was what I -- that was my conclusion that I drew from previous testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I'm not trying to say that you said that in one of your statements. What I'm putting to you now is that due to that; namely, that you called the Serb soldiers -- or, rather, that you used the words "Nazi practices," that there was an incident due to that, and that the Serb soldiers refused to continue participating in the evacuation of refugees, and that that interruption went on for almost one hour. Can you confirm that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot confirm that, because that was the situation that Lieutenant van Duijn described in his statements. And I am -- I never agreed on that, because the Serbs had a clear intention to have a very smooth operations with no interference of DutchBat or whatsoever. So it was clearly the opinion of my colleague, van Duijn. I disagreed then with him, and I disagree still with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I am going to put very simple and short questions to you. We are not talking about opinions here. We are talking about facts. An incident occurred and you used the word "Nazi practices" for that. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I used the word to my colleague van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There was a discussion after that with the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I think this needs a little bit of a clarification. Do I read your answer well, if I understand it that you're stating to us, that you -- when you used the words "Nazi practices," you're addressing your colleague van Duijn and no one else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm addressing to my colleague van Duijn, because I was speaking to my Dutch colleague about it. The so-called Captain Mane was standing near us. That was the situation at that moment, yes. And he could have heard that, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was going to be my next question, whether any of the Serb military there could have heard -- okay. But were you aware of any reaction at the time? Was there a reaction when you use the term "Nazi practices," was there a reaction from any of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no direct reaction. The reaction that I've heard a few minutes later came from the Lieutenant van Duijn himself, and I discussed that with the Colonel Doctor, who was also there in the neighbourhood, Creemer. And I said to him, "What's this kind of situation?" And we talked about that. So that was in fact what happened. But the operation of moving of the deportation of the refugees, in fact, never stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that clears up a few things, yes. Mr. Lazarevic, how much more do you have? How much longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Not more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the answers that you gave to His Honour, the Presiding Judge, you are stating that there was no interruption in the evacuation that went on for about an hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my sight. There was no real stop of the evacuation, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But very soon, after this incident occurred, when you used the words "Nazi practices," you went away from there, right? Just after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only 50 or a 100 metres, and I spoke with the Colonel Dr. Creemer. But I was still watching the line of buses; and still, the work was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the task of the members of DutchBat in the evacuation of refugees from Potocari was to separate groups of refugees, from the masses that were there, into smaller groups of 50 to 60 persons and to check who wanted to go to Srebrenica and who wanted to stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to have V004417 displayed, from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the minutes for the video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just have a look at this. [In English] V004417.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think we should play it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you recognised some of the persons in this video clip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Captain Mane, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On his back, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Van Duijn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And the interpreter, Miki. And you heard just now, and you saw the subtitles, the translation of what Captain Mane is saying to Mr. Van Duijn, or, rather, what he is saying to the interpreter Miki to tell van Duijn in English, that the Dutch Battalion should go amongst the refugees and to see who wants to leave, and that that was their job?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I respectfully there is no foundation for the conclusion that's embedded in that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic, don't you think that Mr. Thayer is correct? If Mane is saying that, it doesn't mean to say that that was so. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, of course not. But on the other hand, I was about to ask the witness whether that's his view, too, after seeing this footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have already asked the witness, and the witness has already given you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but that was before he saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you think the witness is going to change his list mind because Mane ten, 11 years ago, maintained that that was the role of the DutchBat? You are in an optimistic mood today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe because it's Monday, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are usually indulgent on Monday and you are optimistic, so that should work. Yes, let's proceed, Mr. Lazarevic. I think you can move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There are just a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major Rutten, I would like to put a few more questions to you in relation to the evacuation of refugees. Do you know that on the 11th of July 1995, in the evening hours, a meeting was held at the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac between General Mladic and Mr. Karremans, your commander? Do you know that that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion -- well, I know that you did not attend the meeting, but did you have occasion to see the footage of that meeting that was attended by Major Karremans and Mr. Boering on your side and Mladic is there and some other Serb officers? Did you have occasion to see that footage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that footage years later, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And on that video footage, which does exist and which was transcribed, one can clearly hear what the two of them are saying. I'm talking about Karremans and Mladic. Can you confirm that that meeting was held at the request of Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, because I was not in the chain of command then by the Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps who was the first to raise the question of the evacuation of refugees from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any agreement was reached there in Bratunac, on the 11th of July, in the Fontana Hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I give an answer to that, then is it based on the footage that I saw years later, as I just explained to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Then I don't wish to insist on that answer. However, at any rate, one more question in relation to this: Do you know who provided the fuel for the transportation of refugees from Potocari to Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fuel came from DutchBat because it was ordered, I heard later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. I assume that General Mladic could not order the DutchBat to issue fuel. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's your conclusion from here in this courtroom in a safe environment. There, there was a typical psychological warfare going on, if you see the footage more closely. Even after years, you can feel that tension that was in that room. So if you're asking my opinion now or if I agree on that, I would say that they -- General Mladic was clearly in control; and if he could not order it, he had the psychological power to order it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, please allow me to intervene here. Previously, you were asked a question by Mr. Lazarevic, "Do you know who provided the fuel for the transportation of refugees from Potocari to Kladanj?" And your answer was, "The fuel came from DutchBat because it was ordered. This is what we have -- I heard later." This is what we have in the transcript. When you say because it was ordered, I heard later, ordered by whom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Madam Fauveau, we'll have a break in six minutes' time. You can either start now or we can break now, whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do so when the Chamber starts again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I correct what I said. I said I will do what the Chamber wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I heard you say, but then -- oh, yes, okay. No problem. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, given the hour of the day and given our restriction on being able to have any contact with Major Rutten once he's begun testifying, I'm not sure if the estimates for cross-examination are holding. If they are, then I don't believe we'll be able to finish with his testimony today. And I would -- I have no idea whether Major Rutten is available to return tomorrow or any other day in the month of December. So perhaps an inquiry through the witness unit might be appropriate. I just wanted to raise that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Madam Fauveau, how much do you think you're cross-examination will require.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 30 and 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And are you cross-examining the witness? You are? And how long do you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We were first, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, all right. And the Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think I will follow Ms. Condon, who will conduct a rather more substantial cross-examination than I, because this witness affects her client rather more than mine, but I will only be 20, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can say we will finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think you better check with Ms. Condon first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I indicated last week, I think, two hours. I think you appreciate why it has to be that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. No, no. I mean we've told you straight and plain that we were not going to limit you particularly in this case with this witness, you and the Borovcanin. So we need two hours plus another hour, three hours. Major, I was too optimistic. I think you need to make arrangements for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It won't be possible, sir. Tomorrow I'm not available, so I have to attend to another meeting. I'm still working and, I have to do something on my work as well. And tomorrow, it can't be skipped tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when -- let's see. Let's have contact with the victims and witnesses unit, and you will give us information as to your availability; and then we'll decide perhaps, I don't know, we'll have a full hour and a half after the break. Maybe you can try to finish your cross-examination in an hour and a half, with the hope that maybe Madam Fauveau and Mr. Haynes might think it over and opt for not cross-examining this witness. I'm not suggesting. I'm just thinking aloud, but see amongst yourselves a little bit. I think if you make an effort you can finish in an hour and a half, but it's up to you. I don't mean to stop you. So 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I see Ms. Condon standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: We changed the order, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Condon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Major Rutten, I'm going to do my best to conclude my cross-examination of you today, but with the best aim in the world we'll see how we go. I want to ask you some questions about the preparation that you had for your mission to Srebrenica. I recall in your evidence to the van Kemenade inquiry that your view was that you had adequate preparation for the mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Can you tell me the length of the time that you had to prepare, how long did the preparation go for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started in autumn, around September, with the first exercise, and it went on until the second week of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And above and beyond that preparation that you received, you yourself had done some reading on your own, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just preparing what was happening in former Yugoslavia, how the conflict -- the background of the conflict, articles on persons concerning that conflict, some books. I read, for instance, Bridge Over Tara. Just to get a scope of the environment and the conflict itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So, obviously, it would be important for you to inform yourself as much as possible prior to arrival there, is that fair comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. That's a fair comment. It's now standard operation at this moment, to prepare soldiers for the culture where they go into for missions abroad.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Did you, as a result of your own reading that you did, did you form some impressions as to what to expect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not really. Because I read different kinds of sides of the story, and I read also the Saturday News is a lot of paper work with background on the conflict. But also from different kinds of view on different persons from different countries, we have a well-organised, yeah, daily paper here in Holland. And there is a lot of magazines; there is a lot to read on that subject, was there already then, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: In particular, though, I recall you, in your evidence to the parliamentary inquiry, making a comment that you had formed an impression in your own mind about what to expect in enclaves, insofar as what Serbs had been doing, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And can I ask you this? Did you, prior to arrival in Srebrenica, did you have a view of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not as a group. More about the situation they were in.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So you would say that prior to arrival, your mind set was utterly neutral, insofar as Serbs were concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What about when you're on the ground? Did that change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We tried to hold up our impartiality.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Because impartiality was the key to the DutchBat's mission, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Essential to your role --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- was to be neutral, impartial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Sorry, I interrupted you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But we were also human beings so there still -- there happens daily business on either side, which influence you. It's normal, I think. But we spoke that through, in the company, as well as with the battalion, and, yeah, we tried to keep up our impartiality, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you seem to be conceding that that it was often very difficult?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Very difficult, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And in particular, I recall an incident that you talked about in the van - just tell me am I getting the pronunciation wrong with my Australian accent - the Kemenade inquiry; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Kemenade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you recalled an incident, in the context of that conflict with Lieutenant van Duijn, where you had kicked a couple of heavily armed Serb soldiers for no reason other than to show that you didn't like them, that that was what you said to the van --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there is going to be a quote like that coming from counsel, I'd appreciate the witness being shown that exact, alleged statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is from a document that's been recently added to the -- it's 3D49. This is the document that was the subject of the delayed translation. And I'll take you to the reference. Okay. This is at page 26 of 3D49, please. Sorry? Is it 3D50, is it? Sorry, my mistake. Okay. So the Dutch version -- so if we could have the English version, put up, please? Is it not on the system? It hasn't been uploaded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. All right. So is it on Sanction? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can keep yours, and I'm sure the Prosecution will --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Because mine is marked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's one reason. I'm told by my colleague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is 3D50, we have it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You do. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's get 3D50, please, loaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. All right. Here we are. We have it in English on the left, so page 26 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have to work within the limitations that we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: It does not correspond with my page 26, Your Honour, that I'm reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me see, because I --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps page 27. I think it's the next page. If we go to page 27, the passage should be there. Yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, if you have that in front of you, Major?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you'll see that there is a paragraph that begins, "Last week Koster told me about something I did." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Would you like me to read it out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I can read it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Which I don't remember. So that refreshes your memory as to that incident having occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That occurred, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And that's correct, that you did -- well, to be fair to you what you said was you did it for two reasons; that you did it simply to let them know you didn't like them, number 1, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And, secondly, to send a message in relation to the stretchers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. The message it was more related on -- in the situation that was really -- that we were facing there. There were two men, armed, sitting on stretchers, walking around, observing what was happening, sitting on a stretcher, what we could easily use for other means. So that was the situation. And if you asking me now, again, is that like or like not, it has more to do with the situation itself, at this moment. At that specific moment, when something happens, what you're seeing and that image does something with you, so that is what actually happened on the spot. But at the other hand, and that -- I had also a lot of conversations with other Serb soldiers. And they told me where they came from, where they -- what their family was. Some of them told that they had family in Holland, as a refugee, and so and so on. So the same imposed situation as on the Muslim side. So there was no up-front problems from my side with the Serbs as a group. If you -- if you would have asked me that question, yes, I would have answered that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Can I ask you about the preparation in terms of your roles as an intelligence officer, you going over there. I'm not asking you about the tasks themselves, that you were given, but can I ask you this general question? No doubt you were given specific instructions as to the tasks you were expected to perform as an intelligence officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was more or less an intelligence officer from the battalion through the company. So I'm not an intelligence officer by profession, so that means something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right. But prior to your arriving in Srebrenica, was that an expectation, that you would play that role in the battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: It was, yes? So in the course of that expectation, which is what I'm asking you, were there specific instructions, tasks that you were given in order to pursue that role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The specific task was to be a liaison on intelligence matters to the battalion -- from the battalion to the company, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And no doubt that would have entailed being given names of certain officers that you may expect to come into contact with from both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And obviously, it stands to reason, particularly, names of officers that would be performing intelligence functions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Were you -- this is prior to arrival. Were you shown any images or photos of any persons that you may be expected to come into contact with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not prior to the mission, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Not at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you to after the mission. Now, we've already established that you were subject to a number of debriefings, that's correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You had some complaints in terms of the completeness of that process, is that a fair assessment from -- of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the debriefing statement at Assen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And also I think you raised some issues with my learned friend Mr. Josse last week about the Zagreb debriefing as well that was similarly inadequate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, you were interviewed for the NIOD report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's also correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You gave evidence in front of the parliamentary inquiry in 2000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you gave a statement in 1995 for the -- what's known as the Kodak team; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, you also indicate in the van Kemenade inquiry, you make reference to a management report, do you know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Can you tell me about that, please? That's something that you gave a specific statement in relation to, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. It was in the inquiry from the Kodak team. I was asked to -- if I had seen something that could have been subject to a -- to a criminal or other offences that could have happened within the battalion or someone connected to the battalion. And I refused to do that because I would be putting my colleagues in severe problems, but I said it's good to have it investigated. So put it in another kind of report, but not in an official statement that means that they can be prosecuted. Because it was war at that time, so that we have a different situation, and it's good for the organisation, as well as for the person themselves, that it -- that it has been or becomes investigated later on. So that was the meaning of the management report.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. And when did that report -- when was that report released, what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know because the report was drawn up by that Kodak team of the police, the military police. I never got a copy of that report. Later on, in 1998, I remember I saw the first copy of that report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And this was a report that you say was directed to the potential investigation of other members of the DutchBat for criminal activities that may or may -- that they may be responsible for while in Srebrenica and Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possible, yes. Possible criminal activities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you were, as you said, very guarded about giving a full account in the context of that report, because you didn't want to incriminate your colleagues; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, in each of these processes that I've just taken you through; the debriefing -- well, perhaps I'll start with the debriefing in particular. In any of the debriefings that you were subject to by the Ministry of Defence, were you shown photos of -- well, were you shown photos of people that you had come into contact with in Potocari and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No? Were you not asked to provide, in those debriefings, any information that you had gleaned as a result of being an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes,. I was asked to, but the problem was we had almost no photos whatsoever. We had a very poor intelligence situation there with the battalion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But, I mean, you would agree, because I think you even make a reference to it in your -- in the parliamentary inquiry, that even while were you still in Potocari, you were watching Dutch television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You would recall that incident where you're watching Dutch television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you saw General Mladic on television with the scene at Potocari. So there were certainly media reports that you saw while you were still at Potocari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
